Įी सभापित :वह मɇ देख लूंगा। प्रæन संख्या 62। 
Merger of Mid-Day Meal Programme with S.S.A. 
*62. SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have implemented Mid-Day 
Meal programme in the schools in various States; and 
(b) whether it is also a fact that Government propose to merge Mid-
Day Meal programme with Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN R ESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. The Mid-Day Meal Programme is being 
implemented for children at primary stage in schools run by Government 
and Local Bodies, Govt.-aided schools and Education Guarantee Scheme 
and Alternative and Innovative Education centres. 
(b) A proposal is being examined. 
SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: Mr. Chairman, Sir, for implementing the 
Mid-day Meal Programme through the State Governments, the 
Government of India allotted Rs. 1,675 crores for the year 2004-05 and 
Rs. 3,010 crores for the year 2005-06. But, for the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, 
an amount of Rs. 7,165 crores have been allotted. It is for this reason 
that the implementation of the Mid-Day Meal Programme by various States 
is not being done in a proper way. The States are implementing it through 
various agencies; like, in some States, it is done through the Education 
Department, in some States, it is carried out by the Social Welfare 
Department and in other States, it is done through various other 
Departments of the State Government. I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister whether his Ministry is demanding more funds for implementation 
of the Mid-Day Meal Scheme. This is  first part of my supplementary. I 
would also like to know whether the Government would like to have 
uniform implementation of the scheme  by one agency in each State 
instead of giving it to various agencies by various State Governments 
The Government of India may issue guidelines in this regard. 
SHRI ARJUN SINGH: Sir, at the moment, there is no proposal to 
immediately ask for more money because the money provided is being 
utilised, and I don't see any necessity straightway. So far as the guidelines 
are concerned, the guidelines are there. The States have to follow them. 
4 

[28 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
If there is any specific instance given where these guidelines have been 
violated, I will certainly, look into it. 
SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: Sir, my second supplementary is this. The 
merger of the two schemes, namely, the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and the 
Mid-Day Meal Schemes has been opposed in the State Education 
Secretaries' Conference which was called by the hon. Minister because 
they felt that it would not be giving thrust to the Mid-Day Meal Scheme, if 
both the schemes were clubbed together. Sir, the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
and the Mid-Day Meal Scheme are constitutional requirements. But the 
logistics involved and the modalities are different for both the schemes. 
Therefore, I would like to have a categorical assurance from the hon. 
Minister that both the schemes would not be clubbed together. I am asking 
this because it appears that there is  pressure from the Secretariat for 
clubbing the schemes under one head. If these two are clubbed, then, 
the importance of the Mid-Day Meal Scheme will be diluted. Therefore, I 
want the hon. Minister to give an assurance in this House that the Mid-
Day Meal Scheme will be implemented separately. 
SHRI ARJUN SINGH: The fact is that the issue of merger arose out of 
a speech delivered by the hon. Prim e Minister at a meeting of the 
Committee. Since the comment was ma de by the Prime Minister at a 
meeting of the Committee. Since the comment was made by the Prime 
Minister, the whole issue came under  scrutiny, and we thought that it 
would be better that the States looked into that and then we formulated a 
policy. Twenty-one States-have disapproved of it, and the others are also 
in the process of forming their views. We will not change the pattern, as 
it exists today unless we examine all these aspects. It is only then that a

Statement 
(a) to (c) Government has recently issued Policy Guidelines for 
Downlinking of Television Channels, which provide that no person/entity 
shall downlink a channel that has not been registered with the Ministry of 
Information and Broadcasting under these guidelines. It further provides 
all persons/entities desirous of downlinking TV channels shall be required 
to obtain permission from Ministry of  Information and Broadcasting in 
accordance with the terms and conditions prescribed under these 
guidelines. As a result of these guidelines, the local delivery service 
providers i.e. cable operator and DT H service providers will distribute 
only registered TV channels. 
The eligibility criteria prescribed in  the guidelines for the applicant 
company seeking permission to downlink TV channel, inter-alia include: 
• Possessing a net worth of Rs. 1.5 crores and Rs. 1 crore for 
every additional channel. 
• It must be a company registered in India under the Indian Companies 
Act, 1956, irrespective of equity structure, foreign ownership or 
management control. 
• The applicant company must have a commercial presence in India 
with its principal place of business in India. 
• The applicant company to provide details of their Directors and key

Abolition of quota and reservation in private institutions 
*67. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: 
SHRI UDAY PRATAP SINGH: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the Supreme Court of India has recently ruled that 
Government's requirement that the private institutions which do not receive 
any State aid, should also follow Government's policy on reservation of 
seats for the backward classes, is a serious encroachment on the rights 
and autonomy of these institutions; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) Government's reaction thereto and the steps, if any, proposed in 
this regard; 
 
(d) Whether Government have constituted any committee for 
monitoring the fee-structure in the private institutes; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (c) The Supreme Court observed in the case of 
PA. Inamdar and ors. Vs. State of Maharashtra and ors. that the State 
cannot impose its reservation policy on minority and non-minority unaided 
private institutions. According to the order of the Supreme Court neither 
the policy of reservation can be enforced by the State nor any quota or 
percentage of admissions can be carved out to be appropriated by the 
State in a minority or non-minority  unaided private institution. The 
Government is in the process of evolving a common national approach 
to this important issue which addresses national, social and constitutional 
imperatives in a holistic manner. 
28 

[28 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) and (e) The Supreme Court in its judgment in the case of Islamic 
Academy of Education and others Vs. State of Karnataka and others 
have directed the State Governments to constitute a Fee Committee to 
determine the fee structure in unaided institutions in respective States.

Punishment to rapists 
*70. SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: 
SHRI VIJAYJ. DARDA: 
Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that law provides punishment for the proven 
guilt of rape "a minimum of 7 years imprisonment" still many courts have 
30 

[28 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
either awarded lesser years of imprisonment and High Courts have even 
reduced the sentences in such cases; and 
(b) if so, whether Government would ensure that maximum 
punishment, as provided in the law, be awarded in proven cases to deter 
the prospective perpetrators of this heinous crime? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H. R. BHARDWAJ): 
(a) Section 376 of Indian Penal Code (IPC) prescribes a punishment of a 
minimum period of seven years of imprisonment and a maximum 
punishment of life imprisonment for the offence of rape. However, in a 
few serious cases of rapes like rape of a girl below 12 years of age and 
custodial rape, the minimum punishment could be 10 years. As per proviso 
to the above Section, the court may, for adequate and special reasons to 
be mentioned in the judgement, impose a sentence of imprisonment for 
a term less than seven years. 
(b) As the judiciary is independent, it is not possible for the Government 
to interfere in the functioning of the judiciary.

and (b) In order to provide suitable infrastructure and basic amenities in 
the urban areas of the North Eastern States including Sikkim, Ministry of 
Urban Employment and Poverty Alleviation is implementing projects/ 
schemes, since 2001-02, in the urban areas of NER, under 10% Lumpsum

housing, slum upgradation/development and employment generation/

prescribed norms. The State-wise details of projects, sanctioned by this

Professionalisation of Management 
*78. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of HEAVY INDUSTRIES 
AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of heavy industrial undertakings and public enterprises 
where professionalisation of top management has been introduced as a 
policy initiative, and whether the same would percolate down in the 
hierarchy; 
(b) whether there has been any marked gain or improvement in 
performance as a result of this process and how long it would take to 
complete this process in all units of this sector; 
(c) the number of the units already closed, those in operation and 
economic viability of the running units; and 
(d) the future prospects of these units, category-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEAVY 
INDUSTRIES AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN 
DEV): (a) As far as the Central Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) under 
the Department of Heavy Industry are concerned, vacancies are being 
filled as per the policy guidelines for full time and as well as for Independent 
Directors. Policy below the Board level posts is framed by the respective 
PSEs themselves depending upon their professional requirements. 
(b) Filling up of the Board level po sts is a contin uous process and 
actions in anticipation of a vacancy are initiated well in advance to ensure 
timely filling up of such posts. Improvement in performance of a PSE is 
dependent upon a wide range of factors including technology, processes, 
market conditions, status of econ omy, competitivenes s etc. besides 
contribution of the top management on policy initiatives. 
(c) and (d) Out of 48 PSEs under the Department of Heavy Industry, 
11 have been closed and 3 are not in operation. There are 9 profit making 
PSEs and the remaining 25 are incurring loss. Efforts for revival of sick/ 
loss making PSEs through the Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector 
Enterprises (BRPSE) are continuing for improving the viability of the 
enterprises. In the case of 5 PSEs, revival plans have been aproved by 
Government with expectations of sustained viability as projected in their 
revival plans.

452. SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: W ill the Minister of CULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether theatre has traditionally played a very significant role in 
development and propagation of Indian culture; 
(b) the steps taken for the growth of traditional Indian Folk Theatres; 
and

pattern of modern day city life of the country?     
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
(b) and (c) Under the scheme of fi nancial assistance to cultural 
institutions, grants are given to institutions and groups practising traditional 
Indian folk theatres; festivals and performances are held regularly; several 
artists in the field have been hono ured with Sangeet Natak Akademi 
Awards. Audio-Video recordings of many forms have been made. A special 
project is being run for the preservation and development of Koodiyattam, 
a significant tradition of Indian theatre. Under the scheme of 'Assistance 
to Young Theatre Workers', the Sangeet Natak Akademi has funded 
several contemporary plays based on traditional theatres. Programmes 
for promotion of traditional folk theatres are organised in collaboration 
with Zonal Cultural Centres (ZCCs) all over India. The ZCCs have 
introduced a new scheme of Theatre Rejuvenation and for the last three 
years, assistance of Rs. 5.50 lakhs per annum is being provided to each 
of the seven Centres. The ZCCs are also organising festivals of Traditional 
Folk Theatres. Moreover, under the Guru Shishya Parampara Scheme, 
fully funded by Government of India, Traditional Indian Folk Theatres are 
being revived alongwith other folk forms.

and cities.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI KANTI SINGH): (a) and (b) 
As per National Family Health Survey-2, (NFHS-2) (1998-1999) at least

by the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), Ministry of Home Affairs, 
a statement showing the number of cases registered and percentage of

basis of Census 2001 data and the NFHS-2, that nearly 5 crore women 
must be experiencing some form of domestic violence. It has also been 
theorised that a very miniscule pr oportion of the cases experiencing 
domestic violence (1 out of 1000 cases) ultimately get reported. 
(e) The steps taken by the Government to curb domestic violence 
include: 
•   Wide dissemination of information regarding the law enacted to 
create sensitization; 
77

• Setting up of Family Counselling Centres for counselling families 
in situations of domestic violence; 
• Setting up of helplines for women in distress; 
• Support services to victims of violence through schemes such as 
Short Stay Homes and Swadhar under which shelter, maintenance, 
counselling, capacity building, occupational training, medical aid 
and other services are provided; 
• Organizing Legal Literacy and Legal Awareness Camps; 
• Implementations of schemes fo r (i) awareness generation and 
advocacy and (ii) economic empowerment of women through the 
programmes of Rashtriya Mahila Kosh, Swashakti Project, 
Swayamsidha Project, Swawlamban Programme and Support to 
Training and Employment Programme (STEP); 
• Periodic review of laws with a view to remove provisions which 
may be discriminatory to women and to enhance punishments for 
crimes against women as well as enactment of new laws; 
• Sensitization of judiciary and police and civil administration on 
gender issues.

(c) The following main features of Phase II policy are aimed at wider 
participation by private broadcasters:— 
(i) In Phase II, permission shall be granted on the basis of One 
time Entry Fee (OTEF) quoted by the bidders through close tender 
system and annual fee shall be charged@4% of the gross 
revenue for the year or 10% of Reserve OTEF limit for the

discourage speculative bidding it has been prescribed that each 
financial bid shall be accompanied with demand draft of an

selection of successful bidders through open auction, which in 
some cases resulted in speculative bidding and ultimately large-
scale default. The open auction determined the quantum of 
annual license fee, which escalated @ 15% per annum. Phase 
I regime did not provide for adequate safeguards against defaults. 
(ii) No FDI was allowed during Phase I. In Phase II while overall 
foreign investment limit of 20% has been retained, FDI has been 
permitted within this limit subject to certain conditions. 
(iii) In phase I, one entity was eligible for allocation of 1 Channel 
per city if successful in the Open auction. In phase II while each 
applicant shall be allowed to run only one channel per city, total 
number of Channels allocated to entity will be restricted to 15% 
of allocated Channels in the country.

† 548. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that all political parties have recently held 
discussions for evolving consensus on the suggestion given by the election 
commission that persons having more than 2 children should not be allowed 
to contest election; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND JUSTICE 
(SHRI K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) and (b)The Constitution (Seventy-ninth 
Amendment) Bill, 1992 was introduced in Rajya Sabha in December, 1992. 
Under the provisions of the Bill a person shall be disqualified for being 
chosen as, and for being a member of either House of Parliament or the 
Legislative Assembly or, as the case may be, either of the Legislature of the State, 
if he/she has more than two children. However, it will not apply to those who 
already have more than two children or those who beget an additional child 
within one year of the commencement of the Act. The Bill was referred to the 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development for 
examination. The Committee examined the Bill and recommended the Bill for 
passage without any change. 
While recommending the Bill for passage, the Committee also 
recommended that the Government may convene a meeting of leaders of 
various political parties in Parliament to ensure the passage of the Bill.

Accordingly, meetings were held on 14th August, 1997- and 13th 
December, 1999. However, no consensus could emerge in these 
meetings. In the last meeting held on 13th December, 1999, many leaders were 
of the view that the Bill needs to be withdrawn from the Rajya Sabha. This issue 
was discussed in the meeting of the Consultative Committee of the Parliament 
on 2nd May, 2003, where a consensus emerged among the Members on the 
need for more effective measures for controlling population growth in the 
country. It was felt that there was need for larger consensus on the matter, for 
which a meeting of leaders of political parties could be convened. However, 
since the policy of the Government is to keep the family welfare programme 
as voluntary and free from any incentives, disincentives or coercion, the option 
of withdrawing the Bill is under consideration of the Government.

THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH):(a) and 
(c) The tenurial and access rights of forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes in 
165 

RAJYA SABHA [28 November, 2005] 
respect of forest land, which they have been traditionally in-habiting for 
ages have not been adequately recognized under the existing rules and 
guidelines. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs was mandated to formulate a 
comprehensive Central Legislation to redress this historical injustice done 
to the forest dwelling tribal communities and for clear assertion of their 
legal rights on land and other traditional rights. 
This Ministry accordingly prepared a draft "Scheduled Tribes 
(Recognition of Forest Rights) Bill, 2005" to provide a legislative frame 
for recognition of forest rights of the forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes, in 
consultation with the concerned Ministries and other stakeholders. The 
draft Bill proposed to recognize such rights on land, minor forest produce, 
etc. of forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes. The Bill was posted on the website 
of the Ministry seeking comments of the public and all stakeholders till-
10.7.2005. The Ministry has received comments/suggestions from a large 
number of individuals/organizations, either supporting the Bill or opposing 
the same on various grounds. In the light of comments/suggestions 
received, the draft Bill has been further modified to reconcile the twin 
objective of undoing historical injustice done to the tribal communities 
with the concern for environmental protection. The proposed Bill is, 
however, still a tentative draft Bill and to be finalized as per the established 
procedure. No time frame can be i ndicated for its introduction in the 
Parliament.

Concern over the extent of poverty in the country 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA (Maharashtra): Sir, thank you for giving me an 
opportunity to raise my Special Mention. My Special Mention is regarding 
confusion relating to the extent of poverty in India. There is a 40 per cent 
divergence between the poverty estimates of the National Accounts 
Statistics (NAS) and those of the National Survey Organization (NSSO). 
The Planning Commission's poverty estimate of 26 per cent is based on 
the 55th round conducted by NSSO in 1999-2000. If one were to believe 
in the NAS, our poverty levels are down to 15 per cent. Moreover, the 
55th NSS round changed its methodology, giving rise to problems of 
comparability with the earlier rounds. The 50th round of NSS in 1993-94 
estimated poverty of 37 per cent, based on a 30-day recall period for all 
items of consumption. Alongside this 30-day recall method, a separate 
questionnaire was used which deployed different recall periods, 9-day, 
30-day and 365-day. Such anomalies should be addressed and the 
change explained in a transparent manner so that data is neither open to 
political misuse nor it given a distorted view relating to prevalence of the 
extent of poverty in India. Unless a fairly exact extent of poverty is known, 
its effective tackling becomes impracticable leading to wastage of financial 
resources deployed towards mitigat ing poverty, and, simultaneously, 
poverty removal programmes, being launched by the Government, from 
time to time, missing pre-determined targets. In 2000, the World Bank 
did observe that Indian reforms deepened inequality which obviously does 
not square with our high growth rate. The Planning Commission, NSSO 
and NAS must initiate measures immediately to enforce built-in 
safeguards so as to avoid vast difference in arriving poverty figures by 
the surveying authorities.

SHRI PENUMALLIMADHU (Andhra Pradesh): The Supreme Court's 
judgement of August 12, 2005 setting aside the reservation for the 
meritorious and the Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe students in 
the private professional  colleges is beset with serious consequences.

weaker sections of the society w ould not have entry into the private 
professional colleges as hitherto. Because of the special historical factors, 
provisions were made in the Constitution of India for reservation to enable 
the traditionally oppressed classes to catch up with the rest of the society.

commercialisation of higher educ ation where only profit dominates. 
Professional education would hencefo rth be the exclusive privilege of 
the rich.

the civil society, ultimately, disaster management, relief, rehabilitation 
and reconstruction involves partnerships betw een Governments and 
civil society, and it is very important to have at the highest policy-
making authority, at the national level, at the State level and also at the 
district level, since we are having a three-tier structure, representatives 
of a civil society, and I will explain by giving some examples why this is 
of particular importance. Sir, as far as i am concerned, the formation 
of the National Disaster Response Force in chapter VIII of the Bill is a 
very major step forward in disaster management. The Home Minister 
has already said that eight battalions , drawn from various para-military 
outfits, are going to form the 
212 

[28 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
core of the National Disaster Response Force, and I would imagine that 
this would not be a top-down Disaster Management Force. This would 
have field formations, this would be located in strategic parts across the

very difficult, and therefore, we will need a very decentralised way of

is a very major innovation that is proposed in this legislation, I think, it is

as Mr. Ahluwalia said, home guards, you need civilians who are well-

I think, Sir, the second point that I want to make on the Bill is that while 
we have a National Disaster Management Authority, we have a State-
level Disaster Management Authority and we have a District-level Disaster

approach. The real focus is to equip the District Disaster Management

a new suggestion or an observation. He has said that this Bill is applicable 
only to the natural calamities. So, I would like to seek a clarification from 
the hon. Minister because in sub-clause 2(d) of 'Definitions' it is very well 
254 

[28 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
stated that it is man-made as well as natural; I am not going into the 
details of the clause for want of time. It is very specific. If that be the 
case, a rail accident or a bus accident or an accident which occurs due to 
a human negligence, will definitely come within the purview of this term 
'disaster'. So, this Bill will also be applicable to disaster caused by human 
negligence as far as sub-clause 2(d) of 'Definitions' is concerned. 
Sir, I am coming to another point regarding the multiplicity of 
Committees. Sir, when we go through the Bill-this is my apprehension; I 
am only seeking a clarification from the hon.Minister-there are so many 
Committees. There is a National Disaster Management Authority. There 
is an advisory Committee to advise the National Disaster Management 
Authority. Then there is an Executive Committee to assist the National 
Disaster Management Authority. There are so many sub-Committees also. 
There is a multiplicity of Committees. The disaster management activity 
is a voluntary activity. Whenever a contingency arises, whenever an 
exigency arises, we have to act. These activities cannot be done according 
to rules. As per clause 10, the prime responsibility for the implementation 
of the policies of the authorities and the national plan is vested with the

voluntary organisations are taking part in the rescue and rehabilitation 
process, but they do not find any role in this. The bureaucracy is totally 
dominating these Committees. 
Then clause 12 talks about minimum requirements to be provided to

clothing. Food, shelter, medicine sanitation everything is there, but clothing 
is missing here. Clothing is also the primary requirement of the affected 
people. So just like other things clothing should also be given preference 
so far as primary requirements are concerned. Therefore, clothing should 
be incorporated in this clause. 
My next point is about clause 54. It says, "Whoever makes or 
circulates a false alarm or warning as to disaster or its severity or

approach we are taking? We have experienced it so many times. Earlier 
also some predictions were made and subsequently those predictions 
were found to be wrong. Now you may be predicting on the basis of a 
scientific data. Suppose, your prediction proves to be wrong, definitely 
you would be sent to jail. What will happen is, you would not make any 
prediction in future. I would request t he hon. Minister to look into this 
provision.

Response Fund to immediately respond. There is the National Disaster 
Mitigation fund. We are having National Calamity Contingency Fund. We 
are having NCF and the Prime Minister's Distress Relief Fund. There are 
so many funds. I would like to know about the management and 
accounting of these funds. What w ill be the position of the National 
Calamity Contingency Fund? What will be the position of NCF and the 
Prime Minister's Distress Relief fund? The same pattern is going to be 
followed at the State and district levels. They are also collecting money 
and receiving money as response fund and mitigation fund. I would like 
to know about auditing of these funds. 
With these words, I take this opportunity to congratulate the 
Government for coming forward with such a landmark legislation in the 
independent India. Thank you.

are you going to have? Sir, what is this law trying to do? This law is trying 
to make it clear as to how to deal with the disaster when that occurs. 
Disasters occur, and they are enormous. Sometimes, one fumbles. The 
officers, the politicians and those people who are responsible, they are 
over-powered, and they do not know how to cope with the situation. But 
if there is some system established, that system itself will help them, and 
it will help them to reduce the time that is taken today. Now, what happens 
when a disaster takes place? I have personal knowledge because Latur 
disaster taught me so many things . When actually the disaster takes 
place, the first thing we have to do, is to rescue the people. In the Latur 
earthquake, they were under the debris, and when we rescued them, the 
second thing we have to do was to give them the relief. They were without 
clothes, they were without utencils; no food was available, and it was 
necessary to give them food, shelte r, clothing and the things like that. 
So, relief and rescue is the first step which has to be taken by the Local 
Government or the District Authority or any Government, for that matter. 
Supposing, there is no fund available with the people, then it becomes 
difficult. Give them the funds. But enormous amount of money cannot be 
given to the district body or the taluka body or the local body. How many 
villages do we have? 8.5 lakh villages are there. It is not possible to give 
the money to all these villages. But this Fund, a small amount of Fund, 
shall be kept with the district body, which will be utilised to provide rescue 
and relief measures. Nothing more than that. It is going to be a small 
amount. the State Government would be in a position to help the district 
authorities for that purpose. But, at the same time, we are saying, let 
there is a Fund, Rescue and Relief Fund, available with the district body, 
and then the next step is, after the rescue and relief operations are over, 
some kind of interim relief has to be given to them which can continue, 
say for one month or two months, or maybe, one year or two years. Now,

national plan. Now where is the liber ty curtailed? On the contrary, we
